## ✦ IN A NUTSHELL

Tonight's merge watch logged six receipt breaches — but they are not six of the same thing. #2421 and #2446 are the director's own mission-state snapshots: empty PR bodies, zero kernel overlap, merge-faithful — the verdict is a formal breach, and the remediation is a standing snapshot-sync policy or accepting them as self-receipted. #2423 is a mechanical re-stamp with verification notes but no 3-pass structure — formal, with the added finding that its re-stamp basis predates the tip (drift at new tip UNVERIFIED). #2422 merged as [DRAFT] while its own body listed 4 P0 findings — the draft-merge class, which is dangerous in a different way: the branch advertised its own incompleteness and still landed. #2447's attribution is unconfirmed. #2455's delegation claim had no standing record — that one earned a revert (SN-1059), not a retroactive receipt.

The durable rule: **a binary breach/clean verdict treats the director's harmless snapshot and a seat's authority-free semantic merge as the same event — they are not.** Every breach verdict must carry its danger class: formal (process absent, content safe), draft-merge (self-declared incomplete), attribution-unconfirmed, delegation-unrecorded, dangerous (semantic change, no receipt, no valid authority). The class routes the remediation: formal → standing policy or self-receipt; draft-merge → owning lane answers on the board; attribution/delegation gaps → verify before trusting; dangerous → revert by default. A verdict without a class wastes the team's attention on snapshots and under-reacts to the real thing — both errors cost the same currency: Shawn's trust in the watch.

## 🩷 HUMAN NOTE

Shawn — the merge watch logged six receipt breaches overnight, but they're different animals and the verdicts now say so: your two mission-state snapshots (#2421, #2446) are formal breaches — empty bodies, but your own snapshots with zero risky overlap, merge-faithful; the standing answer is a snapshot-sync policy, not alarm. The mechanical re-stamp (#2423) is the same class with one extra finding: it was stamped at an older basis, so drift at the new tip is still unverified. The draft merge (#2422) is its own class — it landed while its own body still said "not done," so the owning lane answers on the board. And #2455's unrecorded delegation claim earned the revert, not a retroactive receipt. Rule banked: every breach verdict now carries its danger class, and the class — not the bare verdict — decides the response. Formal doesn't get alarm; dangerous doesn't get a retroactive receipt.

## 🟣 CHILD NOTE

Imagine a referee who blows the whistle for every foul the same way. One player forgot to tie their shoe (formal foul — no harm). Another ran onto the field before the game started saying "I'm not ready" (draft foul — they announced it themselves). Another played without a signed permission slip (authority foul — the dangerous one). If the referee treats all three the same, the team panics over shoelaces and misses the real problem. The fix: the whistle comes with a label — "shoelace," "not-ready," "no-permission-slip" — and each label has its own fix: tie the shoe, talk to the not-ready player, send the no-slip player off the field. Same whistle, different labels, different fixes.

## 👵 GRANDMA NOTE

It's like a home inspector who marks everything "violation." A missing outlet cover (formal — quick fix, no danger), a contractor who finished while his own punch list still had four items (draft class — he told you it wasn't done and left anyway), and wiring done by someone with no license on file (dangerous — rip it out). If the report says "violation" three times with no labels, you panic about the outlet cover and under-react to the wiring. The fix is simple: every violation gets a label, and the label tells you the fix — labels for the small stuff, and no second chances for the dangerous stuff. Same report, but now you know where to look first.

## 🤖 NAYA NOTE

Note to future me: when I record a merge-law verdict, I ALWAYS name the danger class, never just "breach." Classes: FORMAL (process absent, content verified safe — director's own snapshot, mechanical re-stamp with verification notes) → standing policy or self-receipt, no alarm; DRAFT-MERGE (self-declared incomplete at merge — body lists P0s / "not yet done") → owning lane answers on the board; ATTRIBUTION-UNCONFIRMED / DELEGATION-UNRECORDED (authority claim with no standing record) → verify before trusting, merge lane checks; DANGEROUS (semantic change, no receipt, no valid authority) → revert by default (SN-1059). The binary verdict is the failure mode: it spends alarm on snapshots and leniency on the real thing. Also carry forward the #2423 nuance: a re-stamp certificate is basis-pinned — a merge after its basis re-opens drift (drift at new tip UNVERIFIED), which rides along in the verdict.
